questiontext.text: The word concolic is a blend of which two words?

answer.text: CONCrete + symbOLIC — the program runs on a concrete input while symbolic constraints are collected simultaneously

feedback.text: Correct — concolic execution does both at once: a real concrete run plus symbolic path-condition tracking.

answer.text: CONCurrent + symbOLIC — it runs many symbolic threads in parallel

feedback.text: No — the "conc" is concrete, not concurrent; concolic is about combining concrete and symbolic, not parallelism.

answer.text: CONtrol + logICs — it analyses control-flow logic statically

feedback.text: No — concolic = concrete + symbolic; it is a dynamic technique, not a static control-flow analysis.

answer.text: CONtext + symbOLIC — it tracks contextual symbols only

feedback.text: No — the first part stands for concrete, referring to the real runtime values used alongside the symbolic ones.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic = CONCrete + symbOLIC. The program is executed on an actual concrete input, and at the same time the engine records the symbolic path condition along the path that concrete run takes.

questiontext.text: During concolic execution the engine keeps two states side by side. What are they?

answer.text: A concrete state (actual values driving the real run) and a symbolic state (expressions/constraints over the input symbols)

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete values pick the path actually taken, while the symbolic state records the constraints along it.

answer.text: A source-code state and a compiled-binary state

feedback.text: No — both states describe the running program's data; one is concrete values, the other symbolic expressions.

answer.text: A pass state and a fail state of the test oracle

feedback.text: No — the two states are concrete and symbolic; pass/fail is a separate testing concern.

answer.text: Two independent random states used for statistical sampling

feedback.text: No — one state is a real concrete run, the other is a symbolic constraint state; neither is a random sample of the other.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic execution maintains a concrete state (the actual values, which deterministically select the path the run takes) alongside a symbolic state (the variable-to-expression map and the path condition collected along that same path).

questiontext.text: In concolic execution, the path condition recorded during a run is:

answer.text: The conjunction of the branch conditions taken along the single path that the concrete input actually drove

feedback.text: Correct — because a concrete run follows exactly one path, the path condition describes that one executed path.

answer.text: The disjunction of all path conditions of every path in the program

feedback.text: No — a concolic run records only the one path the concrete input took, as a conjunction of its branch outcomes.

answer.text: A count of how many branches the program contains

feedback.text: No — the path condition is a logical formula over the inputs, not a branch count.

answer.text: The concrete output value the program returned

feedback.text: No — it is the constraints on the inputs along the executed path, not the output.

generalfeedback.text: Because the concrete input drives exactly one path, the engine collects the branch conditions taken on that path and conjoins them into the path condition — a formula over the symbolic inputs characterizing that executed path.

questiontext.text: After a concolic run records a path condition, how does the engine try to reach a new, not-yet-covered path?

answer.text: It negates one branch condition in the recorded path condition and asks the solver for an input satisfying the modified constraint

feedback.text: Correct — flipping one branch and solving yields a concrete input that drives execution the other way at that branch.

answer.text: It recompiles the program with that branch removed

feedback.text: No — the program is never modified; only the path condition is altered and re-solved.

answer.text: It keeps re-running the same concrete input until a different path appears

feedback.text: No — a deterministic program on the same input always takes the same path; the engine negates a branch and solves for a new input.

answer.text: It negates every branch at once and solves the whole thing

feedback.text: No — the standard step flips one branch (typically the last unnegated one) while keeping the prefix, then solves.

generalfeedback.text: The engine picks a branch condition on the recorded path, negates it (keeping the constraints before it), and hands the modified path condition to a solver; the satisfying assignment is the next concrete input, which drives execution down the sibling path.

questiontext.text: Which sequence best describes one iteration of the concolic testing loop?

answer.text: Run on a concrete input → record the path condition → negate a branch → solve → the solution is the next concrete input

feedback.text: Correct — this concrete-run / record / negate / solve cycle repeats to explore new paths.

answer.text: Solve a random constraint → compile → run → discard the result

feedback.text: No — concolic starts from a concrete run, records the real path condition, then negates and solves; nothing is discarded and no compilation step is involved.

answer.text: Enumerate all paths statically → solve each → pick the shortest

feedback.text: No — concolic is dynamic: it drives one concrete run at a time and steers to new paths by branch negation.

answer.text: Mutate the source code → re-run the tests → measure coverage

feedback.text: No — that is mutation testing; concolic negates branch constraints and solves for inputs, leaving the code unchanged.

generalfeedback.text: The concolic loop: pick a concrete input (often random at first), execute it, record the path condition of the path taken, negate one branch condition, solve the modified constraint to obtain the next concrete input, and repeat — driving execution down new paths each time.

questiontext.text: DART, one of the original concolic tools, stands for:

answer.text: Directed Automated Random Testing

feedback.text: Correct — DART directs random testing using the symbolic path condition to reach new paths.

answer.text: Dynamic Abstract Refinement Testing

feedback.text: No — DART stands for Directed Automated Random Testing.

answer.text: Deterministic Assertion Regression Tool

feedback.text: No — DART is Directed Automated Random Testing, a concolic engine.

answer.text: Distributed Analysis of Runtime Traces

feedback.text: No — DART is Directed Automated Random Testing.

generalfeedback.text: DART (Directed Automated Random Testing) starts from random concrete inputs and uses the collected symbolic path condition to direct subsequent inputs toward uncovered branches — coining the concolic approach.

questiontext.text: CUTE, a well-known concolic tool, stands for:

answer.text: Concolic Unit Testing Engine

feedback.text: Correct — CUTE applies concolic execution to unit testing, including code with pointers.

answer.text: Constraint-based Uniform Test Explorer

feedback.text: No — CUTE stands for Concolic Unit Testing Engine.

answer.text: Coverage Under Test Estimator

feedback.text: No — CUTE is the Concolic Unit Testing Engine.

answer.text: Combined Unit & Type Evaluator

feedback.text: No — CUTE is the Concolic Unit Testing Engine.

generalfeedback.text: CUTE (Concolic Unit Testing Engine) brought concolic execution to C unit testing, notably handling pointer/data-structure inputs by combining concrete and symbolic reasoning.

name.text: Why keep a concrete input alongside the symbolic state

questiontext.text: A key reason concolic execution keeps a concrete input alongside the symbolic state is that when a constraint cannot be solved (e.g. it involves an external call), the engine can substitute the concrete value observed at runtime and keep going.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete value is a ready fallback that lets execution continue where pure symbolic reasoning would stall.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: This is precisely a central advantage of concolic execution: the concrete run supplies a real value to substitute when a symbolic term is unsolvable.

generalfeedback.text: Keeping a concrete input means the engine always has a real observed value for every expression. When a symbolic term is too hard, nonlinear, or opaque (an external/native call), it substitutes the concrete value and continues — something pure symbolic execution cannot do.

questiontext.text: Where does the very first concrete input in a concolic run typically come from?

answer.text: It is chosen arbitrarily, often randomly — the loop then refines subsequent inputs by solving negated path conditions

feedback.text: Correct — the seed input can be random; the engine improves coverage from there by directed branch flipping.

answer.text: It must be a value proved optimal by the solver before any run

feedback.text: No — the first input needs no proof; it is typically just a random seed that starts the loop.

answer.text: It is always zero for every input variable

feedback.text: No — while a fixed seed is possible, the point is that the first input is arbitrary/random, not a mandated zero.

answer.text: It is derived by static analysis of the whole program first

feedback.text: No — concolic is dynamic; it simply starts from a concrete (often random) input rather than a static pre-analysis.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic execution bootstraps from an arbitrary, often random, concrete input (this is the "Random" in DART). Each later input is computed by negating a branch on the previous run's path condition and solving.

questiontext.text: Because it uses a concrete input, a single concolic run follows exactly one execution path (in a deterministic program).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — concrete values deterministically select one path; that is why the run records a single path condition.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A concrete input in a deterministic program takes exactly one path; concolic reaches other paths only by solving negated constraints on later runs.

generalfeedback.text: Each concolic run is a real execution on concrete values, so it takes one path and records that path's condition. New paths are reached across iterations by branch negation and re-solving, not within a single run.

name.text: Role of the solver in concolic

questiontext.text: What does the constraint/SMT solver do in the concolic loop?

answer.text: It solves the modified (partly negated) path condition to produce the next concrete input

feedback.text: Correct — the solver's satisfying assignment becomes the concrete input for the next run.

answer.text: It executes the program on the concrete input

feedback.text: No — running the program is done by the (instrumented) execution; the solver only computes inputs from constraints.

answer.text: It decides whether the test's output is correct

feedback.text: No — that is the oracle's job; the solver produces inputs, not verdicts.

answer.text: It measures branch coverage of the suite

feedback.text: No — coverage tracking is separate; the solver turns a negated path condition into a concrete input.

generalfeedback.text: After the engine negates a branch, it hands the modified path condition to the solver; a satisfying assignment is exactly the concrete input that will drive the next run down the newly targeted path (or UNSAT if that path is infeasible).

questiontext.text: Which best captures how concolic execution differs from pure symbolic execution?

answer.text: Concolic always has a real concrete run alongside the symbolic state, so it can substitute concrete values when the symbolic reasoning gets stuck

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete run is the safety net that lets concolic proceed past unsolvable terms.

answer.text: Concolic never uses a solver, while pure symbolic always does

feedback.text: No — concolic relies on a solver to flip branches; the difference is the accompanying concrete run.

answer.text: Pure symbolic runs the program concretely, concolic does not

feedback.text: No — it is the reverse: concolic performs real concrete runs; pure symbolic does not.

answer.text: Concolic guarantees full path coverage, pure symbolic does not

feedback.text: No — neither guarantees full coverage; both face path explosion. The real distinction is the concrete companion run.

generalfeedback.text: Both track a symbolic path condition and use a solver. The concolic difference is the simultaneous concrete run: it supplies a real value to fall back on when a constraint is unsolvable, nonlinear, or involves an opaque external call.

questiontext.text: Concolic tools instrument the program under test primarily in order to:

answer.text: Observe, during the concrete run, the branch conditions taken and build the symbolic path condition in parallel

feedback.text: Correct — instrumentation collects the symbolic constraints alongside the real execution.

answer.text: Slow the program down so the solver has time to think

feedback.text: No — instrumentation exists to gather symbolic constraints during the run, not to add delay.

answer.text: Replace all branches with random coin flips

feedback.text: No — branches are observed and recorded symbolically; they are not replaced by randomness.

answer.text: Permanently rewrite the program to a bug-free version

feedback.text: No — instrumentation only records information for the analysis; it does not fix the program.

generalfeedback.text: The program is instrumented so that, as the concrete input drives execution, the engine simultaneously records each branch condition symbolically and accumulates the path condition — the raw material for the negate-and-solve step.

questiontext.text: Every path that a concolic run explores corresponds to a real execution on a concrete input, so concolic execution reports no false (infeasible) paths.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — each concolic step is an actual concrete run, so the paths it reports are genuinely executable (this is its soundness with respect to explored paths).

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Because every explored path is driven by a concrete input that really runs, concolic execution does not manufacture infeasible paths.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic execution actually runs the program on each generated concrete input, so any path it reports as explored is genuinely feasible. Its limitation is completeness (it may miss some paths), not soundness of the paths it does explore.

name.text: What picks the path a run takes

questiontext.text: In a single concolic run, what determines which one path through the program is taken?

answer.text: The concrete input values, which are executed for real and select each branch outcome deterministically

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete state drives the actual run and thus fixes the path; the symbolic state just records it.

answer.text: The solver, which chooses a path before the run begins

feedback.text: No — within a run the concrete values pick the path; the solver only computes inputs for future runs.

answer.text: The path condition, which forces execution down a chosen branch

feedback.text: No — the path condition is recorded from the run; it does not steer the current concrete execution.

answer.text: A random choice made at each branch

feedback.text: No — branches are decided by the concrete values, not by randomness during the run.

generalfeedback.text: The concrete input is really executed, so at each branch the concrete values decide true/false and thus fix the single path taken. The symbolic side merely records that path's condition for later branch negation.

name.text: Trace: single if, record the PC

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void f(int x) {
  if (x > 5) error();   // branch B1
}

The concolic run starts with concrete input x = 0. What path condition does this run record?

answer.text: x ≤ 5 (the false side of B1, since 0 > 5 is false)

feedback.text: Correct — x = 0 makes x > 5 false, so the run takes the false branch and records x ≤ 5.

answer.text: x > 5 (the true side of B1)

feedback.text: No — x = 0 does not satisfy x > 5, so the run takes the false branch and records x ≤ 5, not x > 5.

answer.text: x == 0 (the concrete value)

feedback.text: No — the path condition records the branch outcome (x ≤ 5), not the specific concrete value used.

answer.text: true (no constraint, because no branch was taken)

feedback.text: No — the branch B1 was evaluated; its false outcome contributes the constraint x ≤ 5.

generalfeedback.text: With x = 0, the condition x > 5 evaluates false, so the run follows the false branch. The engine records the negation of the branch condition it did not take, i.e. the constraint actually satisfied: x ≤ 5.

name.text: Trace: negate and solve for next input

questiontext.text:
Same code:

void f(int x) {
  if (x > 5) error();   // branch B1
}

The first run used x = 0 and recorded x ≤ 5. To cover the other side of B1, the engine negates it. Which next concrete input could the solver return?

answer.text: x = 6 (any value satisfying the negated constraint x > 5)

feedback.text: Correct — negating x ≤ 5 gives x > 5, and x = 6 satisfies it, driving the run into error().
No — 5 > 5 is false, so x = 5 still takes the false branch and does not cover the other side.
No — -1 does not satisfy x > 5; it would re-take the already-covered false branch.

answer.text: No input exists; the negated constraint is unsatisfiable

feedback.text: No — x > 5 is easily satisfiable (e.g. x = 6), so the path is feasible.

generalfeedback.text: Negating the recorded constraint x ≤ 5 yields x > 5. The solver returns any satisfying value (e.g. x = 6), which becomes the next concrete input and drives execution into error().

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void g(int x) {
  if (x == 42) bug();   // branch B1
}

The run starts with x = 7 (so B1 is false, PC is x ≠ 42). What next input does negating B1 yield?

answer.text: x = 42 — negating x ≠ 42 gives x == 42, whose only solution is 42

feedback.text: Correct — the solver computes the exact value 42, immediately reaching bug().

answer.text: x = 43 — any nearby value works

feedback.text: No — the negated constraint is the equality x == 42, so 43 does not satisfy it; only 42 does.

answer.text: x = 7 — the run keeps the same input

feedback.text: No — x = 7 gives the already-covered false branch; the engine solves the flipped equality for 42.

answer.text: No solution; equalities cannot be negated

feedback.text: No — negating x ≠ 42 is simply x == 42, which the solver satisfies with x = 42.

generalfeedback.text: The first run's constraint is x ≠ 42; negating it gives x == 42. The solver returns exactly x = 42 — the classic case where concolic/symbolic reasoning beats random testing, which would almost never guess 42.

questiontext.text: A run took branches in order [B1: true, B2: true], giving path condition c1 ∧ c2. Using the usual depth-first strategy (flip the last unnegated branch first), what is the next path condition to solve?

answer.text: c1 ∧ ¬c2 — keep the prefix c1, negate the last branch c2

feedback.text: Correct — depth-first flips the deepest (last) branch first while preserving the earlier decisions.

answer.text: ¬c1 ∧ c2 — negate the first branch, keep the second

feedback.text: No — that flips B1 first; depth-first negates the last branch (c2) before backtracking to earlier ones.

answer.text: ¬c1 ∧ ¬c2 — negate both branches

feedback.text: No — each step negates exactly one branch; here the last one, giving c1 ∧ ¬c2.

answer.text: c1 ∧ c2 — re-solve the same condition

feedback.text: No — re-solving the same condition re-covers the same path; the engine flips c2 to reach a new one.

generalfeedback.text: Depth-first exploration negates the last unnegated branch condition while keeping the prefix intact: from c1 ∧ c2 it forms c1 ∧ ¬c2. Only after exhausting the c1-prefix subtree does it backtrack and flip c1.

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void h(int a, int b) {
  if (a > 0)          // B1
    if (b > 0)        // B2
      target();
}

Run 1 uses a = 1, b = -1: B1 true, B2 false, PC = (a > 0) ∧ (b ≤ 0). Flipping the last branch (B2), what input reaches target()?

answer.text: a = 1, b = 1 — satisfies (a > 0) ∧ (b > 0)

feedback.text: Correct — keeping a > 0 and negating b ≤ 0 to b > 0 gives a path into target(); a = 1, b = 1 works.

answer.text: a = -1, b = 1 — satisfies b > 0

feedback.text: No — a = -1 fails a > 0, so B1 is false and target() is never reached; the prefix a > 0 must be kept.

answer.text: a = 1, b = 0 — b is non-negative

feedback.text: No — b > 0 requires strictly positive b; b = 0 fails, so B2 stays false.

answer.text: a = 0, b = 0 — both zero

feedback.text: No — a = 0 fails a > 0; the negated constraint keeps the prefix a > 0 and flips b to b > 0.

generalfeedback.text: Flipping B2 forms (a > 0) ∧ (b > 0): the prefix a > 0 is preserved and b ≤ 0 is negated to b > 0. The solver returns any satisfying pair, e.g. a = 1, b = 1, which drives execution into target().

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void k(int x) {
  int y = x + 3;
  if (y == 10) hit();   // B1
}

Run 1 uses x = 0 (so y = 3, B1 false). Negating B1, what next input does the solver return?

answer.text: x = 7 — the constraint over the input is x + 3 == 10

feedback.text: Correct — y is the expression x + 3, so B1 becomes x + 3 == 10, giving x = 7.

answer.text: x = 10 — the branch tests == 10

feedback.text: No — the branch tests y == 10 where y = x + 3, so the constraint on the input is x + 3 == 10, i.e. x = 7.

answer.text: x = 3 — matches the first computed y

feedback.text: No — x = 3 gives y = 6, not 10; solving x + 3 == 10 gives x = 7.

answer.text: y = 10 — treat y as the free input

feedback.text: No — y is not an input; it is the expression x + 3, which must be substituted, yielding x = 7.

generalfeedback.text: The symbolic state records y = x + 3, so the branch y == 10 is the constraint x + 3 == 10 over the actual input x. Negating the false outcome and solving gives x = 7.

name.text: Concolic vs pure symbolic on a simple case

questiontext.text: For if (x > 5) error(); with a solvable linear guard, how do concolic and pure symbolic execution compare on reaching error()?

answer.text: Both reach it — each solves x > 5 (concolic after negating the branch on its first concrete run) — the concrete companion matters only when a constraint is unsolvable

feedback.text: Correct — on a simple solvable guard the two behave similarly; the concrete fallback distinguishes them only for hard/opaque constraints.

answer.text: Only pure symbolic can reach it; concolic cannot solve inequalities

feedback.text: No — concolic uses the same solver and easily handles x > 5 by negating the branch and solving.

answer.text: Only concolic can reach it; pure symbolic cannot solve inequalities

feedback.text: No — pure symbolic solves linear inequalities fine; both reach error() here.

answer.text: Neither can reach it without random luck

feedback.text: No — both solve x > 5 exactly; no luck is required for a simple linear constraint.

generalfeedback.text: When every constraint is solvable, concolic and pure symbolic reach the same paths; both solve x > 5 directly. The concrete-value fallback only becomes decisive when a constraint is nonlinear, unsolvable, or involves an opaque external call.

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void m(int x) {
  if (x < 100) a();   // B1
  else b();
}

The concrete run uses x = 250. Which literal does the engine conjoin into the path condition for B1?

answer.text: x ≥ 100 — the run took the else branch, so the satisfied condition is the negation of x < 100

feedback.text: Correct — with x = 250 the guard x < 100 is false, so the recorded literal is x ≥ 100.

answer.text: x < 100 — the branch's written condition

feedback.text: No — the written condition is false for x = 250; the engine records the outcome actually taken, x ≥ 100.

answer.text: x == 250 — the concrete value

feedback.text: No — the path condition records the branch outcome (x ≥ 100), not the specific concrete number.

answer.text: Nothing — else branches contribute no constraint

feedback.text: No — taking the else branch contributes the negated guard x ≥ 100 to the path condition.

generalfeedback.text: The path condition always records the outcome actually taken. With x = 250 the guard x < 100 is false, so the engine conjoins its negation, x ≥ 100, into the path condition.

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void p(int x) {
  if (x > 0)        // B1
    if (x < 0)      // B2
      dead();
}

Run 1 uses x = 5: B1 true, B2 false, PC = (x > 0) ∧ (x ≥ 0). What happens when the engine flips B2 to try to reach dead()?

answer.text: The flipped condition (x > 0) ∧ (x < 0) is UNSAT, so the solver returns no input and the engine skips that infeasible path

feedback.text: Correct — no x is both positive and negative, so dead() is unreachable and correctly generates no test.

answer.text: The solver returns x = 0, reaching dead()

feedback.text: No — x = 0 satisfies neither x > 0 nor x < 0; the conjunction is unsatisfiable.

answer.text: The engine substitutes a concrete value and reaches dead() anyway

feedback.text: No — concrete fallback is for unsolvable/opaque terms, not for a cleanly UNSAT linear constraint; the path is genuinely infeasible.

answer.text: The program is modified to make the path feasible

feedback.text: No — concolic never modifies the program; an UNSAT flip simply yields no input.

generalfeedback.text: Flipping B2 while keeping the prefix gives (x > 0) ∧ (x < 0), which is UNSAT. The solver reports no solution, so the engine skips this infeasible path — dead() is correctly never targeted.

name.text: Trace: number of runs to cover both branches

questiontext.text: For a single if (x > 5) A(); else B(); with both sides feasible, how many concolic runs are needed to cover both branches, starting from one arbitrary concrete input?

answer.text: 2 — one run covers the branch the seed takes; negating it and solving gives a second input covering the other

feedback.text: Correct — one seed run plus one negate-and-solve run covers both sides.

answer.text: 1 — a single run covers both branches

feedback.text: No — a concrete run takes only one side; the other needs a second input from a negated constraint.

answer.text: 4 — every branch needs two runs

feedback.text: No — a single two-way branch needs just two runs total, one per side.

answer.text: Unbounded — random seeds may never hit both

feedback.text: No — concolic is directed: it solves the negated constraint deterministically, so two runs suffice.

generalfeedback.text: The seed run covers whichever side its concrete value takes. Negating that branch and solving yields a second input for the opposite side. Two runs cover both branches — the directedness that distinguishes concolic from blind random testing.

questiontext.text: Consider a branch whose recorded (satisfied) condition on run 1 is (x + y < 4). Negating it, which input pair does the solver accept?

answer.text: x = 3, y = 3 — satisfies the negation x + y ≥ 4

feedback.text: Correct — 3 + 3 = 6 ≥ 4, so this pair takes the flipped branch.

answer.text: x = 1, y = 1 — small values

feedback.text: No — 1 + 1 = 2 < 4 still satisfies the original condition, not its negation.

answer.text: x = 0, y = 3 — sums to 3

feedback.text: No — 0 + 3 = 3 < 4, which fails the negated constraint x + y ≥ 4.

answer.text: x = 2, y = 1 — sums to 3

feedback.text: No — 2 + 1 = 3 < 4, so this stays on the original branch.

generalfeedback.text: Negating x + y < 4 gives x + y ≥ 4. Only x = 3, y = 3 (sum 6) satisfies it; the other options all sum to less than 4.

name.text: Trace: input to keep prefix, flip deeper branch

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void q(int a, int b) {
  if (a == b)       // B1
    if (a > 10)     // B2
      z();
}

Run 1 uses a = 3, b = 3: B1 true, B2 false, PC = (a == b) ∧ (a ≤ 10). Flipping B2 to reach z(), which input works?

answer.text: a = 11, b = 11 — keeps a == b and satisfies a > 10

feedback.text: Correct — the prefix a == b is preserved and a ≤ 10 is negated to a > 10; a = b = 11 satisfies both.

answer.text: a = 11, b = 3 — a > 10 holds

feedback.text: No — a ≠ b breaks the preserved prefix a == b, so B1 is false and z() is unreachable.

answer.text: a = 5, b = 5 — equal values

feedback.text: No — a = 5 fails the negated constraint a > 10, so B2 stays false.

answer.text: a = 10, b = 10 — right at the boundary

feedback.text: No — a > 10 is strict; a = 10 fails it, so z() is not reached.

generalfeedback.text: Flipping B2 forms (a == b) ∧ (a > 10): keep a == b, negate a ≤ 10 to a > 10. The pair a = 11, b = 11 satisfies both constraints and drives execution into z().

name.text: Why re-running the same input fails to explore

questiontext.text: Why can't a concolic engine reach a new path by simply running the same concrete input again?

answer.text: A deterministic program takes the same path for the same input, so a new path requires a new input from a negated-and-solved constraint

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly why the engine negates a branch and solves for a different input.

answer.text: Re-running clears the symbolic state, losing the path condition

feedback.text: No — the reason is determinism: same input, same path; the engine must change the input to change the path.

answer.text: The solver forbids reusing any concrete input

feedback.text: No — there is no such prohibition; the point is that the same input simply retraces the same path.

answer.text: Repeated runs randomly pick different branches

feedback.text: No — a deterministic program does not pick branches randomly; identical input yields the identical path.

generalfeedback.text: For a deterministic program, the concrete input fully determines the path taken. To explore a different path the engine must supply a different input — obtained by negating a branch on the recorded path condition and solving.

questiontext.text: For if (a) {...} if (b) {...} (two independent branches), starting from a run with a=false, b=false and flipping the last branch first, which is a plausible order of path conditions the engine solves next?

answer.text: First ¬a ∧ b (flip the last branch), then a ∧ ... (backtrack to flip the first)

feedback.text: Correct — depth-first flips the deepest branch (b) before backtracking to the earlier one (a).

answer.text: First a ∧ b only, ignoring the other combinations

feedback.text: No — depth-first explores more than one combination; it starts by flipping the last branch to ¬a ∧ b.

answer.text: It solves ¬a ∧ ¬b, the same as the seed run

feedback.text: No — that is the already-covered seed path; the engine flips a branch to reach a new one.

answer.text: It must flip both branches simultaneously first

feedback.text: No — each step flips exactly one branch; the deepest first under depth-first order.

generalfeedback.text: Depth-first flips the last branch first: from ¬a ∧ ¬b it forms ¬a ∧ b, then after that subtree backtracks to flip the first branch (a ∧ ...). Each step negates a single branch while keeping the prefix.

name.text: Concrete values keep the prefix consistent

questiontext.text: When the engine negates the last branch, it keeps the earlier branch conditions unchanged so that the solved input still reaches that branch point.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — preserving the prefix ensures the new input actually reaches the flipped branch before diverging.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The prefix is preserved precisely so the new input follows the same route up to the flipped branch, then diverges there.

generalfeedback.text: To reach a sibling of a deep branch, the input must first satisfy all the earlier decisions leading to it. So the engine keeps the prefix constraints and negates only the target branch, then solves the whole conjunction.

name.text: Concrete fallback for an external call

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void r(int x) {
  int h = opaque_hash(x);   // native/library, no symbolic model
  if (h == 1234) win();     // B1
}

Where a pure symbolic engine gets stuck, how does concolic execution proceed at B1?

answer.text: It substitutes the concrete value of h observed at runtime, so B1 becomes a concrete true/false and execution continues down a real path

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete run always has an actual h, so concolic keeps going where pure symbolic stalls on the unmodeled call.

answer.text: It builds a full symbolic model of opaque_hash automatically

feedback.text: No — the call is opaque with no model; concolic sidesteps this by using the concrete observed value, not by modeling it.

answer.text: It aborts, exactly like pure symbolic execution

feedback.text: No — the whole point of the concrete companion is to continue past the opaque call rather than abort.

answer.text: It proves B1 unreachable

feedback.text: No — it does not prove anything about B1; it simply plugs in the concrete h and follows the resulting real path.

generalfeedback.text: Because opaque_hash has no symbolic model, its symbolic result is unknown. Concolic execution uses the concrete value of h that the actual run produced, so B1 evaluates concretely and execution proceeds along a genuine path — the key advantage over pure symbolic execution, which would stall.

questiontext.text: When concolic execution substitutes a concrete value for an unsolvable/opaque term, what is the cost?

answer.text: Incompleteness — by fixing that term to one concrete value, the engine may fail to explore other feasible paths that depend on it

feedback.text: Correct — the fallback keeps execution going but can hide paths reachable only for other values of the opaque term.

answer.text: Unsoundness — it may report paths that cannot actually run

feedback.text: No — every run is concrete and real, so soundness of explored paths is preserved; the cost is missed paths (completeness).

answer.text: It always crashes the solver

feedback.text: No — substituting a concrete value simplifies the constraint; it does not crash the solver.

answer.text: There is no cost; coverage is unaffected

feedback.text: No — pinning the opaque term to one value can prevent reaching alternative paths, an incompleteness cost.

generalfeedback.text: Concrete fallback preserves soundness (paths explored are real) but sacrifices completeness: fixing an opaque term to the one observed concrete value can mask branches feasible only under other values of that term, so some paths may never be explored.

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void s(int x, int y) {
  if (x * y == 30)   // B1, nonlinear
    t();
}

Run 1 uses x = 6, y = 4 (so x*y = 24, B1 false). If the solver cannot handle the nonlinear flip, how can concolic still make progress?

answer.text: Fix one variable to its concrete value (e.g. x = 6) so the constraint becomes linear (6*y == 30 → y = 5), then solve

feedback.text: Correct — pinning x to its concrete value linearises the constraint, letting the solver find y = 5 and reach t().

answer.text: Give up entirely, since nonlinear constraints are undecidable

feedback.text: No — concolic uses the concrete value of one operand to simplify to a solvable linear constraint rather than giving up.

answer.text: Randomly guess both x and y until x*y == 30

feedback.text: No — the concolic approach pins one operand concretely and solves the resulting linear equation; that is the point of the concrete companion.

answer.text: Modify the program to remove the multiplication

feedback.text: No — the program is never modified; the concrete value of x is substituted to simplify the constraint.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic execution substitutes the concrete value of one operand (x = 6), turning x*y == 30 into the linear 6*y == 30, which the solver satisfies with y = 5. Running x = 6, y = 5 reaches t(). The cost is incompleteness: with x pinned to 6 it may miss solutions like x = 5, y = 6.

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly characterises concolic execution's guarantees?

answer.text: The paths it explores are all real (sound), but it may miss some feasible paths (incomplete)

feedback.text: Correct — real concrete runs guarantee no false paths, while concrete fallback and bounding can leave paths unexplored.

answer.text: It explores every feasible path (complete) but may report some that cannot run (unsound)

feedback.text: No — it is the opposite: sound on explored paths, but not guaranteed complete.

answer.text: It is both fully sound and fully complete for all programs

feedback.text: No — path explosion and concrete fallback mean completeness is not guaranteed.

answer.text: It is neither sound nor complete

feedback.text: No — because every explored path is a real execution, it is sound with respect to the paths it reports.

generalfeedback.text: Every concolic step is a genuine concrete execution, so the paths it explores are real (soundness of explored paths — no false positives from infeasible paths). But concrete fallback for opaque/nonlinear terms and bounded search mean it may not reach every feasible path (incompleteness).

name.text: Path explosion is managed, not eliminated

questiontext.text: How does concolic execution relate to path explosion?

answer.text: It still faces path explosion and manages it with a search strategy and iteration/depth limits, rather than eliminating it

feedback.text: Correct — concolic does not remove the exponential path growth; it bounds exploration to cope.

answer.text: It eliminates path explosion entirely by using concrete inputs

feedback.text: No — using concrete inputs does not remove the exponential number of branch combinations; concolic still must bound its search.

answer.text: It has no notion of paths, so path explosion does not apply

feedback.text: No — concolic explicitly explores paths by branch flipping, so path explosion very much applies.

answer.text: Path explosion only affects random testing, not concolic

feedback.text: No — path explosion is a core challenge for all path-based techniques, concolic included.

generalfeedback.text: Each branch flip can lead to more branches, so the number of paths still grows exponentially. Concolic manages this with search heuristics (depth-first, coverage-guided) and bounds on iterations, loop unrolling, or depth — but it does not eliminate path explosion.

name.text: Multi-branch trace: naming each next input (1)

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void f(int a, int b) {
  if (a > 0)          // B1
    if (b == a + 1)   // B2
      target();
}

Seed run: a = -1, b = 0 (B1 false). Under depth-first flipping, what is the input for the run that first makes B1 true (flipping B1)?

answer.text: Any a > 0 with b unconstrained, e.g. a = 1, b = 0 — solving the single constraint a > 0

feedback.text: Correct — flipping B1 only imposes a > 0; B2 is not yet on the recorded path, so b is free (e.g. b = 0).

answer.text: a = 1, b = 2 — must already satisfy B2 as well

feedback.text: No — when flipping B1, only a > 0 is required; B2 has not been recorded yet, so b need not satisfy b == a + 1 at this step.

answer.text: a = -1, b = 0 — reuse the seed

feedback.text: No — the seed has B1 false; flipping B1 requires a > 0, so the input must change.

answer.text: No input works; a > 0 is unsatisfiable

feedback.text: No — a > 0 is trivially satisfiable, e.g. a = 1.

generalfeedback.text: The seed took B1 false, so its path condition is just a ≤ 0. Negating it gives a > 0, the only constraint at this step (B2 was never reached). The solver returns any a > 0, e.g. a = 1, b = 0.

name.text: Multi-branch trace: naming each next input (2)

questiontext.text: Continuing the previous snippet, the run a = 1, b = 0 now takes B1 true and B2 false (0 ≠ 2), with PC = (a > 0) ∧ (b ≠ a + 1). Flipping B2, which input reaches target()?

answer.text: a = 1, b = 2 — keeps a > 0 and satisfies b == a + 1

feedback.text: Correct — preserve a > 0, negate b ≠ a + 1 to b == a + 1; with a = 1 that means b = 2.

answer.text: a = 1, b = 1 — b unchanged from a step earlier

feedback.text: No — b must equal a + 1 = 2; b = 1 fails the flipped constraint.

answer.text: a = 0, b = 1 — b == a + 1 holds

feedback.text: No — a = 0 breaks the preserved prefix a > 0, so B1 becomes false and target() is unreachable.

answer.text: a = 2, b = 2 — both equal

feedback.text: No — with a = 2, b == a + 1 requires b = 3, not 2.

generalfeedback.text: Flipping B2 gives (a > 0) ∧ (b == a + 1). Keeping a = 1 from the prefix, b must be a + 1 = 2. The input a = 1, b = 2 reaches target(). (The solver could also pick another a > 0 with matching b.)

questiontext.text: For the nested snippet if (a > 0) if (b == a + 1) target();, starting from seed a = -1, b = 0, how many concolic runs (including the seed) are needed to first reach target(), flipping one branch per iteration depth-first?

answer.text: 3 — seed (B1 false), then B1 true/B2 false, then B1 true/B2 true reaching target()

feedback.text: Correct — one flip is needed to enter B1, another to satisfy B2, so the third run hits target().

answer.text: 2 — the seed plus one flip reaches target()

feedback.text: No — the seed fails B1; one flip only makes B1 true (B2 still false), so a second flip is needed, giving three runs.

answer.text: 1 — the seed reaches target() directly

feedback.text: No — the seed has a = -1, failing B1 immediately, so it cannot reach target().

answer.text: 4 — each nesting level doubles the runs

feedback.text: No — this particular path needs exactly two branch flips after the seed, i.e. three runs, not four.

generalfeedback.text: Run 1 (seed a=-1): B1 false. Run 2 (a=1,b=0): flip B1 → B1 true, B2 false. Run 3 (a=1,b=2): flip B2 → both true, reaching target(). Three runs in total.

questiontext.text: To keep concolic exploration finite on a loop whose count depends on input, a common approach is to:

answer.text: Impose a bound — e.g. a depth/iteration limit or bounded loop unrolling — accepting that paths beyond the bound go unexplored

feedback.text: Correct — bounding trades completeness for termination, a standard path-explosion control.

answer.text: Negate every loop-body branch at once to cover all iterations in one run

feedback.text: No — a single run covers one path; loops are handled by bounding the exploration, not by simultaneous negation.

answer.text: Prove the loop terminates and then skip it

feedback.text: No — skipping the loop would miss its behavior; the loop is bounded/unrolled instead.

answer.text: Switch to pure symbolic execution, which has no path explosion

feedback.text: No — pure symbolic execution also suffers path explosion; switching does not solve it.

generalfeedback.text: A symbolic loop count can spawn unboundedly many paths, so engines cap exploration with an iteration/depth limit or bounded unrolling (and search heuristics). This keeps the run finite at the price of not exploring paths beyond the bound — an accepted incompleteness.

questiontext.text: CUTE extended concolic testing to programs with pointers and dynamic data structures by:

answer.text: Tracking a symbolic representation of the heap/pointer structure alongside concrete pointers, and solving pointer constraints (e.g. aliasing, null-ness) as well as scalar ones

feedback.text: Correct — CUTE handles both a logical input map for scalars and a structure for pointer inputs, using the concrete run to resolve what the solver cannot.

answer.text: Forbidding all pointer inputs so only integers are tested

feedback.text: No — CUTE's contribution was precisely to support pointer and data-structure inputs, not to forbid them.

answer.text: Converting the whole program to a pointer-free form before testing

feedback.text: No — CUTE reasons about pointers directly, using concrete values where symbolic reasoning is insufficient.

answer.text: Running only pure symbolic execution on the heap

feedback.text: No — CUTE is concolic: it combines concrete pointer values with symbolic constraints, which is what makes heap inputs tractable.

generalfeedback.text: CUTE (Concolic Unit Testing Engine) represents pointer inputs with a logical structure and generates both scalar values and pointer shapes (including aliasing and null cases). The concrete run provides real pointers to fall back on, letting it test functions over dynamic data structures.

questiontext.text: Even when concolic execution substitutes concrete values for terms the solver cannot handle, the paths it actually executes remain genuinely feasible (no false paths are introduced).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — substitution uses the value from a real run, so the resulting execution is still a real, feasible path.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Concrete fallback never fabricates a path; it uses observed values, so every executed path remains real. The tradeoff is missed paths, not false ones.

generalfeedback.text: Because the substituted value comes from an actual execution, the path the engine then follows is one the program really can take. Soundness of explored paths is preserved; only completeness (some feasible paths may be skipped) is at risk.

name.text: Divergence when a constraint is approximated

questiontext.text: Suppose concolic execution pins an opaque term to a concrete value and solves for a new input, but on re-running, execution takes a different branch than predicted (a "divergence"). What does the engine do?

answer.text: It detects the divergence from the actual concrete run and records the real path taken, since the concrete execution is always the ground truth

feedback.text: Correct — the concrete run is authoritative, so a divergence is simply observed and the true path recorded, keeping the analysis sound.

answer.text: It trusts the predicted path and ignores the actual run

feedback.text: No — the concrete run is ground truth; the engine records the path actually executed, not the predicted one.

answer.text: It reports the predicted path as covered even though it was not taken

feedback.text: No — that would be unsound; the engine relies on the real run, which reveals the divergence.

answer.text: It crashes because the prediction was wrong

feedback.text: No — divergence is handled gracefully by observing the actual concrete run and continuing.

generalfeedback.text: Divergences can happen when a substituted/approximated term makes the solved input take an unexpected path. Because concolic always executes concretely, it observes the real path and records it — the concrete run is the ground truth, preserving soundness even when a prediction was off.

name.text: Multi-branch trace with a concrete-fallback step

questiontext.text:
Consider:

void w(int x) {
  int t = external(x);   // opaque; run observed t = 3 for x = 2
  if (x > 0)             // B1
    if (t == 3)          // B2, depends on opaque t
      goal();
}

Run 1 uses x = 2: B1 true, and t = 3 so B2 true — goal() is reached. Is the path to goal() reported, and is it real?

answer.text: Yes and yes — the concrete run actually reached goal(), so the path is reported and is genuinely feasible; B2 used the concrete t = 3

feedback.text: Correct — concolic uses the observed t, so goal() is really reached and soundly reported.

answer.text: No — B2 depends on an opaque call, so concolic cannot report the path

feedback.text: No — concolic uses the concrete t = 3, so it evaluates B2 and really reaches goal(); the path is reported.

answer.text: Yes but it may be a false path, since t is opaque

feedback.text: No — the run truly executed to goal(), so the path is real, not false; opacity affects completeness, not this run's reality.

answer.text: The engine must abort at the opaque call

feedback.text: No — that is pure symbolic behavior; concolic proceeds using the observed t = 3.

generalfeedback.text: The concrete run computed t = 3 from external(2) and really executed through B1 and B2 into goal(). Concolic reports this genuinely feasible path. What it cannot easily do is force B2 the other way for other x, since the relationship between x and t is opaque — an incompleteness, not an unsoundness.

questiontext.text: Why do concolic engines use search strategies (depth-first, coverage-guided, random path) rather than exhaustively exploring all paths?

answer.text: Because the path space is exponential (path explosion), a strategy prioritises which branches to flip within a limited budget

feedback.text: Correct — with too many paths to try all, the strategy decides where to spend limited solver/run budget.

answer.text: Because the solver can only answer one query per program

feedback.text: No — solvers answer many queries; the reason for strategies is the exponential number of paths.

answer.text: Because concrete runs are not repeatable

feedback.text: No — concrete runs are repeatable; strategies exist to cope with the huge path space.

answer.text: Because branch negation is impossible without a strategy

feedback.text: No — negation works regardless; a strategy just chooses which negation to pursue next given the path explosion.

generalfeedback.text: Exhaustive exploration is infeasible because branches and loops make the path count exponential. Search strategies (depth-first, coverage-guided, generational, random-path) choose which branch to flip next so the limited budget of runs and solver calls targets useful, uncovered paths.

name.text: Concolic does not guarantee full coverage

questiontext.text: Concolic execution guarantees that, given enough time, it will cover every feasible path of any program.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Incorrect — concrete fallback for opaque/nonlinear terms and bounding for loops mean some feasible paths may never be reached.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — concolic does not guarantee full path coverage; concrete fallback and bounded search can leave feasible paths unexplored.

generalfeedback.text: Concolic execution manages path explosion with bounds and heuristics and falls back to concrete values for terms it cannot solve. Both can prevent it from reaching every feasible path, so full coverage is not guaranteed — though every path it does explore is real.
